## Work

### amber — DevOps Engineer, SDE1 (Dec 2024 – Present)

- Sole DevOps engineer for 8+ months, owning production AWS infrastructure for 50+ services and 50,000+ monthly active users across global environments.
- Run EKS workloads through Helm and ArgoCD with autoscaling and resource tuning, lifting cluster utilization by 24%.
- Built CI/CD in Argo Workflows, Jenkins, and GitHub Actions, moving deployments from a few a week to several a day.
- Codified infrastructure with Terraform across 4 AWS accounts using reusable modules and remote state, eliminating configuration drift.
- Held production to 3–4 incidents, each detected and resolved inside 5 minutes, backed by SLO alerting in Grafana, Prometheus, and CloudWatch plus blameless post-mortems.

Tools: AWS, EKS, Terraform, ArgoCD, Karpenter, Grafana, FinOps

#### Case study: ECS to EKS migration (2026)

Moving 50+ services from ECS and EC2 onto EKS, with just-in-time nodes and a zero-downtime cutover.

Before:

50+ containerized and non-containerized services were split between AWS ECS and hand-managed EC2. Scaling followed CPU and memory, which lagged behind the queue-driven load many of those services actually had.

What changed:

- Stood up EKS with managed node groups, IRSA-based pod identity, and VPC CNI networking.
- Karpenter provisions On-Demand and Spot node pools just in time, with SQS-driven interruption handling.
- KEDA scales event-driven workloads on queue depth where CPU/memory HPA fell short.
- Cut over blue-green, shifting traffic behind the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

Numbers:

- 50+: services migrated to EKS
- 0: minutes of customer-facing downtime

Stack: Amazon EKS, ECS, Karpenter, KEDA, Terraform, Helm, Docker, AWS LB Controller

#### Case study: AWS cost optimization (2025)

A company-wide programme over two and a half months that cut monthly AWS spend by 45%, roughly $200K a year.

Before:

Monthly AWS spend sat at $35–38K. Aurora ran Serverless, Redshift dc2.large nodes tied 2 TB of storage to compute, Fargate ran everything On-Demand, 14 Application Load Balancers each fronted a handful of services, and SQS consumers short-polled empty queues.

What changed:

- Data tier: Aurora Serverless to provisioned r7g Graviton; Redis re-platformed to Valkey on Graviton; Redshift dc2.large to RA3, decoupling 2 TB of storage from compute; heavy Athena scans rerouted to a right-sized database.
- Compute: ECS Fargate to EC2 Graviton, with Spot for fault-tolerant jobs, and self-hosted CI runners.
- Networking: 14 ALBs consolidated to 4; SQS consumers moved to long-polling.
- Commitments last: Compute Savings Plans layered on once capacity was predictable.

Numbers:

- −45%: monthly AWS spend
- $200K/yr: saved ($35–38K → $19–21K a month)
- 14 → 4: Application Load Balancers
- −90%: SQS costs, via long-polling
- 0: impact on availability

Stack: Graviton, Spot, Savings Plans, Aurora, Redshift RA3, Valkey, Cost Explorer

#### Case study: Agentic CI/CD failure triage (2026)

A Kubernetes-native agent that reads failed builds, works out the root cause, and fixes or retries 40% of them on its own.

Before:

30+ pipelines across Jenkins and Argo Workflows served 40 services. Every red build meant a person opening the job, scrolling the log, and deciding whether it was real or just flaky.

What changed:

- An LLM layer parses job logs, classifies each failure by root cause, and posts a Slack summary with the recommended fix.
- Closed-loop remediation opens targeted GitHub pull requests for code and config defects, and retries transient failures through a Jenkins MCP server.
- The same agent reviews Terraform and Helm pull requests against Well-Architected, security, and cost guardrails, and runs scheduled drift and hygiene audits.
- Alert-driven self-healing (rollbacks, restarts, scaling, cordon/drain) runs behind Slack approval gates for high-risk actions, with a full audit log, shipped as an RBAC-scoped Helm chart.

Numbers:

- 40%: of failures resolved hands-free
- −70%: mean triage time
- 8+ h/wk: of engineering time returned
- 30+: pipelines watched

Stack: Python, LLM Agents, MCP, Jenkins, Argo Workflows, Helm, Slack

## Posts

### Why I Traded My Portfolio Template for Newsprint

Published 2026-10-26. Field Notes. 364 words. URL: https://rajatdev.fun/threads/notes-from-a-homelab/

> A short note on serving this site from a box at home, and on why the weird, independent web is worth the trouble.

The previous version of this site was a single page of frosted-glass cards floating over an animated aurora. It was well built, and it looked like every other developer portfolio on the internet, mine included. It said "please hire me" very politely (and it did sometimes work), but it didn't say much else.

This version is a page of type on cream paper, and the change was mostly about what a page is allowed to contain.

#### A portfolio is a pitch

A portfolio has one job, so everything on it has to serve that job. A personal site doesn't. The engineering is still here, in full, on [the builds page](/builds/). But the front page is also allowed to mention a Camus novel and a motorbike ride down the Konkan coast, and there's a [whole page for books and rabbit holes](/threads/). Those things are true about me too, and the template had no place to put them.

#### The box

This site is served from a machine from my home. A request for it goes through Cloudflare's edge, down an encrypted tunnel, over an ordinary residential fibre line, through a reverse proxy, and into a container on a bare-metal Linux host. What comes back is a folder of static HTML that Astro built ahead of time.

There is no database and no server-side code, so the box barely notices visitors. You can see [its readings](/builds/#homelab) on the builds page. The uptime guarantee is simple: if you can read this, it is up.

#### Why bother

Hosting it myself is not the cheapest way to put a website online, and it's certainly not the easiest. But the address is mine, the hardware is mine, and nobody's algorithm decides who sees it. If the site breaks, it breaks because of something I did, which also means I can fix it, which does keep happening. 

The independent web runs on people doing slightly impractical things with their own corner of it: blogs with strange layouts, digital gardens, sites that are just a list of the books someone liked. This is my corner. And it could be something else entirely the next time you visit, so keep visiting.

Thanks for reading.

### How to Cut an AWS Bill by 45% Without Anyone Noticing

Published 2026-09-14. Infrastructure. 925 words. URL: https://rajatdev.fun/threads/how-to-cut-your-aws-bill-by-45-percent/

> Two and a half months, roughly $200K a year, and not one customer-facing change. A field guide to cutting a cloud bill quietly.

The bill was somewhere between $35,000 and $38,000 a month. Two and a half months later it was between $18,000 and $20,000, which works out to roughly $200,000 a year. Availability didn't change, nobody shipped a feature differently, and nobody outside the team noticed anything, which was the point.

Cost work gets a bad name because it is usually done loudly: a freeze on new resources, existing apps running slow, a spreadsheet of blame, and arguing about tags. Most of the money was going to things nobody had looked at since they were created. And we did not achieve this by simply buying out the AWS servers in advance.

#### Rule one: commitments go last

The tempting first move and the lowest hanging fruit of them all is always to buy Savings Plans and Reservations, It is what most of the consultants in the field suggest, because it is one click and the discount is large. It is also the move that locks in whatever waste you already have, for one to three years. If you commit to the spend of an over-provisioned fleet, you have made the waste cheaper rather than removing it.

So the order was: right-size, re-platform, consolidate, and only then commit, once capacity had settled into something predictable.

#### The data tier

The databases were the biggest line, and the most interesting.

- **Aurora Serverless to provisioned Graviton.** Serverless is a good deal when load is spiky or unknown. Understanding where our spikes came from was a crucial task, we spent some time looking at the usage graphs, the website traffic goes up drastically during the evening but the database spikes did not show the same pattern, it looked rather like some crons were running. We looked removed heavy crons, looked at the most time consuming queries and built and index for their tables, a few optimizations in the code and we had a system where the load predictable. And a steady workload on Serverless pays a premium for elasticity it never uses, so it moved to provisioned r7g instances. Further down the road we changed the storage to I/O Optimized as our data storage was rathr less but the TPM was slightly high which worked greatly in ur favour.
- **Redis to Valkey, on Graviton.** Valkey was launched by AWS on AWS as an answer to the pricing model of Redis, it is esentially just a fork of redis when it was free. Now at the time of writing this page I hear that redis has again put out their new version with a free pricing. Although AWS has kind of now locked in the people who migrated to valkey by selling reservations tied to the engine, we have little incentive to go back to Redis anyways.
- **Redshift dc2.large to RA3.** The dc2 family bundles storage with compute so if your data warehouse requires more storage you've got buy RAM and CPU as well, so holding about 2 TB of data meant paying for compute just to have somewhere to keep it. RA3 separates the two and moving to it made huge sense.
- **Heavy Athena scans, rerouted.** Athena bills by data scanned. And we had so many automations which started small but as time went by the data kept piling up, and just in a few years we had hundreds of automations scanning TBs of data per day, queries kept scanning the same large datasets over and over; We created right-sized database put in the seeded the data into it and now the automations run at fraction of the cost. We were even able to turn off the database when the automations were not runing.

#### Compute

ECS Fargate which is publicized as a serverless, and an all time running server is lovely until you read the invoice, escpecially when you are restricted to only use x86 processors. I moved the all our ECS services to EC2 on Graviton, with Spot capacity for the jobs that can survive an interruption. 

#### The assassinations

There were 14 Application Load Balancers. Each one carries an hourly charge whether it serves a million requests or none, and most of ours fronted a single small service.

An ALB listener can route by host header and path to many target groups, so one load balancer can do the job of several. Fourteen became four.

> Nobody files a ticket about a load balancer that no longer exists. That is the whole trick.

#### The quiet one: SQS long-polling

Short polling returns immediately, usually with nothing in it, and every empty receive is a billed request. Consumers that poll in a tight loop run up a surprising bill for doing nothing. Long-polling makes the request wait for a message instead:

```hcl
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "jobs" {
  name                      = "jobs"
  receive_wait_time_seconds = 20 # long-poll: far fewer empty, billed receives
}
```

That one setting cut SQS costs by about 90%.

---

#### Then, and only then, the commitment

With the the architecture settled, the fleet right-sized, and the system optimized the remaining baseline was steady enough to commit to. Compute Savings Plans went on last, sized to what was actually left.
The databases, elasticache, and elasticSearch nodes were now reserved, instances and lambdas shared the saving plans.

The billing dashboard has not been the same since. Even 
after 1.5 years of scaling out and growing we still haven't every crossed the 25K USD mark. Writing the prcess down does make me feel like we had to know a lot of stuff and get everything right at each step, but the process itself was super easy, just look at the bill, get your pain points ready, and start with the largest and highest impact ones to the smallest.
